title: Detune the traps: strain shifts midgap defect levels off resonance
idea: A sitar player detunes the sympathetic strings so they stop ringing along; likewise, wrap the storage-node depletion region in a local stressor (about 1 GPa compressive SiN liner or an embedded Si:C pocket) so the dominant generation centers (divacancy, V-O, interstitial Fe) shift a few tens of meV away from midgap. SRH generation falls roughly as exp(-|Et-Ei|/kT), so a 40-60 meV detune cuts their current about 4-7x at 85 C. The stress level is picked from DLTS-under-uniaxial-stress data, and the stressor is kept clear of the access channel so Vt does not move.
why: Fact 3: the tail cells are dominated by single near-midgap centers. A 4-7x lower tail current means 3-6x longer tREFW and refresh energy cut by the same factor, with no new channel material.

title: Tin-doped storage junctions trap vacancies before they form leakage centers
idea: This borrows probiotic competitive exclusion, where harmless microbes take the niche pathogens need. Co-implant isovalent Sn (about 1e19 cm-3) into the storage-junction depletion zone so that Sn-vacancy pairs, which are electrically benign, capture the vacancies made by the storage-node implant before they can build divacancies or P-V E-centers near midgap. This is the chemistry that makes Sn-doped silicon radiation-hard in particle detectors. It costs one low-dose implant that activates in the existing junction anneal.
why: Fact 3: vacancy-related midgap centers from implant damage are a major source of tail cells. The aim is 3-10x fewer tail cells and 2-4x relaxed refresh, with one implant and no new tools.

title: Skin-graft spare capacitor antifused onto each tile's weakest cell
idea: Surgeons graft healthy tissue exactly where a wound is weakest. Here each 16-cell neighborhood gets one spare storage capacitor whose plug sits beside the 16 storage contacts behind thin high-barrier antifuse links. At sort, the link to the neighborhood's worst-retention cell is blown, so that cell's capacitance and charge budget double in place. The address map, ECC and sense path are untouched.
why: Facts 1 and 3: tREFW is set by the 1e-5 to 1e-6 retention tail. Doubling Cs of the worst cell in each neighborhood clips that tail, allowing about 2x longer refresh interval (roughly 50% less refresh energy) for about 6% more capacitor area.

title: Boustrophedon active layout keeps passing wordlines off storage nodes
idea: Boustrophedon script reverses direction on every line. Do the same with the active-area tiling: mirror alternate active rows and re-pair the bitline contacts so that, wherever a buried wordline passes through isolation as a neighbor's passing gate, it is bordered by a shared bitline-contact junction rather than a storage-node junction. Storage junctions then face only their own gate and plain STI, which removes the passing-gate inversion/GIDL path. The cost is a modified landing-pad pattern and roughly 5-8% cell area.
why: Facts 3 and 9: passing-gate leakage and passing-gate hammer coupling are top retention and row-hammer contributors. Removing the adjacency could cut tail leakage 2-5x and raise the hammer threshold, with no new materials.

title: Studio star-grounding for wordline off-rails kills bounce-driven leakage bursts
idea: Audio engineers kill hum by star-grounding, so that no two return currents share a wire. Apply this to the array: give every sub-wordline-driver stripe its own low-impedance return strap to the VNWL and VBB regulators, plus local MOS decoupling, instead of a shared mesh. Then, when hundreds of wordlines switch in a refresh or activation burst, the unselected local wordlines and the p-well stop bouncing 50-100 mV toward turn-on, and the activity-dependent subthreshold leakage bursts this causes in every access transistor of the mat disappear.
why: Fact 3: off-current rises about 10x per 70-80 mV of off-rail bounce during each burst. Removing the bounce takes out a hidden, load-dependent tail component, which could relax refresh guard bands about 1.5-2x under heavy traffic.

title: Aircraft static wicks bleed plasma charge from storage nodes during etch
idea: Aircraft trailing-edge static wicks bleed charge away before it can arc. During the 60-75:1 capacitor-hole etch, the etch front opens onto the landing pads and dumps plasma charging current through the storage contacts into the storage-node junctions. Make the bottom layer of the capacitor mold a weakly conductive film (doped poly or TiN etch-stop) strapped to the substrate at the mat edge, so each pad is bled to ground the moment it opens, then oxidize the film to an insulator after the etch.
why: Facts 3 and 4: charging damage at storage junctions leaves latent trap sites that later appear as tail and VRT cells. The target is 2-3x fewer tail cells from one mold-stack change.

title: Brass water key: periodic hole drain for floating-body vertical access transistors
idea: Trumpeters open a water key to dump the condensate that would otherwise choke the horn. In 4F2 vertical-channel and lateral 3D DRAM access transistors, the body floats, so holes from GIDL and impact ionization pile up after access bursts, lower Vt and raise off-current (gate-induced floating-body effect). Add a gated p+ drain line along each pillar row's base, touching the bodies once per 64 pillars. It opens only during refresh slots to drain the holes, so it adds no static junction leakage while idle.
why: Facts 2 and 3: body charge-up can raise off-current 10-100x after bursts in 4F2 and 3D cells. A periodic drain restores intrinsic retention for about 1-2% area and helps 3D cells reach DRAM retention.

title: Sepsis source control: diode-free charge pumps stop substrate carrier injection
idea: Sepsis care removes the infected source instead of treating every downstream organ. Negative VBB/VNWL pumps built from diode-connected stages, and high-field sense-amp and sub-wordline-driver FETs, forward-bias junctions or impact-ionize, injecting minority carriers that diffuse tens of microns into the nearby mats. Rebuild the pumps as cross-coupled, bulk-switched triple-well stages whose junctions can never forward-bias, and give the driver FETs drain-extended layouts, so the injection is removed at its source rather than guarded against.
why: Facts 3 and 7: tail cells in edge rows near pumps and drivers could fall 2-3x, and fewer guard rings and dummy rows give back periphery area.

title: Deep-plough implants bury end-of-range loops below the depletion region
idea: Farmers deep-plough to bury weed seeds below the depth where they can sprout. The storage-node implant's end-of-range dislocation loops normally land inside the junction depletion region, where they generate leakage. Use a deeper Si or Ge pre-amorphization (for example 60 nm instead of 15 nm) and a solid-phase regrowth sequence that parks the loops 20-30 nm below the depletion edge in neutral silicon, where they are electrically harmless, while the dopant profile stays shallow.
why: Fact 3: implant end-of-range defects are a classic source of junction leakage. Relocating them out of the depletion region could cut the junction-limited tail 2-4x with existing tools.

title: Concert-hall bass traps for silicon: phononic superlattice starves thermal generation
idea: Acousticians tame a boomy hall by trapping the specific frequencies that build up. Thermal emission from a deep trap requires absorbing several phonons, so surround the storage-node depletion region with a Si/Si:C or Si/SiGe superlattice whose phonon minigaps suppress the modes that couple most strongly to the dominant trap, slowing its emission rate. The first test is DLTS on one known center, compared inside and outside a phononic superlattice.
why: Fact 3: if emission rates drop even 2-3x, tail leakage and refresh drop by the same factor. This would be a new lever on the leakage tail that is independent of bandgap and passivation.

title: Wine racking for 3D DRAM: volatilize germanium residues off released channels
idea: Winemakers rack wine off its lees so the sediment cannot spoil it. After the SiGe sacrificial layers of a lateral 3D DRAM stack are etched away, Ge atoms stay on and just under the released silicon channel surfaces, narrowing the local bandgap and adding interface states. Before gate oxidation, run a racking step that grows a thin oxide and then anneals in vacuum at 500-600 C, so GeO2 plus Ge leaves as volatile GeO, stripping residual Ge from every tier at once.
why: Facts 2 and 3: Ge residues raise access-transistor off-current in stacked tiers. Removing them could cut tier leakage 2-5x and help lateral 3D cells meet retention without lower operating temperature.

title: Athermal capacitor dielectric stops pyroelectric charge drift during thermal bursts
idea: Telescope builders design athermal optics so focus does not drift as the night cools. ZrO2/HZO capacitor films often hold polar orthorhombic grains with an electrode-imprinted net polarization, so a 10-20 K temperature swing during a workload burst pyroelectrically moves hundreds to about 1,500 electrons onto or off each 5 fF storage node. That is a hidden charge loss that is not leakage. Measure it on test arrays, then suppress it with a non-polar phase recipe (monoclinic or amorphous interlayer) and symmetric electrodes that remove the imprint.
why: Facts 1 and 3: a cell holds only about 30k electrons, so a pyroelectric loss of up to about 5% during bursts eats sense margin. Removing it recovers 5-10% retention margin and a temperature-transient failure mode.

title: Water-tower charge banks let refresh fire twice as many rows
idea: Towns refill water towers slowly overnight so morning demand never exceeds pump capacity. At 32-64 Gb, tRFC is set by how many rows the VPP pumps and the package current limit can activate at once. Place deep-trench capacitor towers of about 1-2 nF per bank beside the wordline drivers. The pumps trickle-charge them between refresh commands, and they discharge during each REF, so each refresh activates 2x the rows without exceeding pump or IDD limits.
why: Fact 3: refresh blocks 10-20% of bandwidth at 32-64 Gb. Halving tRFC halves that loss, for about 1% of die area in trench capacitors.

title: Swap the dopant cultivar: gallium p-wells avoid boron-oxygen defects
idea: Banana growers switched cultivars when a blight targeted one variety, and solar makers did the same, replacing boron with gallium to eliminate the boron-oxygen complexes that form under carrier injection. In DRAM p-wells built in oxygen-rich CZ silicon, carriers injected by GIDL, hammering and periphery activity can likewise create B-O recombination centers next to storage junctions. Dope the array p-well and access channel with gallium, which forms no B-O complex, using the existing implanters.
why: Facts 3 and 9: this removes one activity-triggered source of new tail cells over product life, with a projected 1.5-2x lower tail in hot, heavily accessed parts. The gallium mass used is negligible.

title: Drug-interaction check: hydrogen anneals also neutralize channel boron, lowering Vt
idea: Pharmacists check whether one drug undoes another. The hydrogen anneal that passivates interface traps also pairs atomic H with boron acceptors in the access channel and p-well. That neutralizes part of the doping and lowers Vt unevenly from cell to cell, which raises subthreshold leakage. Add a short reverse-biased bake at 150-200 C after passivation: it dissociates the weakly bound B-H pairs and sweeps the H away while leaving the stronger Si-H interface bonds intact.
why: Fact 3: if B-H pairing lowers Vt by tens of mV in some cells, reactivation could cut the subthreshold part of the tail 2-5x with one low-temperature step.

title: Thermal-bridge fix: nitride supporter lattice leaks between storage nodes
idea: Building scientists found that steel studs bridging the insulation leak most of a wall's heat. The silicon-nitride supporter lattice that braces tall capacitor pillars touches neighboring bottom electrodes, and Poole-Frenkel conduction through nitride under the roughly 1 V between a '1' neighbor and a '0' neighbor forms a data-dependent leakage path from storage node to storage node. Skin the supporter with ALD SiO2/Al2O3 where it meets the electrodes, or make it from carbon-doped oxide, to break the bridge.
why: Facts 1 and 3: as pillars grow taller and supporters thinner, this path matters for tail cells. Cutting it removes a data-pattern-dependent tail component (about 1.5-2x for the affected cells).

title: Hydrogen-line lesson: hyperfine-free silicon-28 slows spin-allowed thermal generation
idea: Radio astronomy's 21-cm line exists because electron and nuclear spins couple through the hyperfine interaction. Part of trap-assisted generation in silicon runs through spin-correlated pairs whose triplet states stay blocked until hyperfine fields from 29Si nuclei mix them. Growing the array's active layer as isotopically enriched 28Si epi (under 0.01% 29Si) removes that mixing, so spin-blocked pathways stay blocked longer and the spin-dependent fraction of tail and VRT generation falls.
why: Fact 3: a speculative but testable lever. If the spin-dependent share of tail generation is large, tail leakage falls by that share, and 28Si also conducts heat about 10% better.

title: Catcher's framing: plate dip at wordline turn-off cancels kickback loss
idea: A catcher pulls the glove back toward the strike zone at the instant of the catch. When a row closes, the falling wordline's kickback steals about 5-10% of each stored '1' voltage. Dip that row group's plate segment by dV just before the wordline falls and restore it just after: the closing row is isolated while the plate is low and gains a dV fraction that cancels the kickback, while rows that were already isolated see a down-and-back pulse with zero net effect.
why: Facts 1 and 10: recovering 5-10% of stored voltage lengthens retention about 10-20% and widens sense margin, using plate segmentation and no new material.

title: Keep iron partnered: preserve Fe-B pairs that sit far from midgap
idea: Like pair skaters who are steadier together than apart, residual interstitial iron in p-type silicon is a strong near-midgap generation center alone but a far weaker one when paired with boron. Shape the p-well so boron is plentiful exactly where iron collects. Add a 100 C pairing soak after solder reflow, which dissociates the pairs, and keep minority-carrier injection away from arrays, so the iron stays paired through product life.
why: Fact 3: from its SRH level offset, paired iron should generate on the order of 100x less than isolated interstitial iron at 85 C. Keeping the pairs could cut iron-related tail cells several-fold without removing any iron.

title: Triage interrupts the elective case: pausable refresh yields to urgent reads
idea: Hospitals pause an elective procedure at a safe point when a trauma case arrives. Make REF interruptible at row-group boundaries: when a read targets a refreshing bank, the in-DRAM refresh engine finishes its current row group, raises a 'paused' flag, serves the read, then resumes from its saved counter. A hard deadline forces completion before the tREFI slack runs out.
why: Fact 3: refresh lock-out adds hundreds of ns to tail read latency and costs 10-20% bandwidth at 32-64 Gb. Pausing removes most of the latency penalty without touching retention.

title: Theatre 'in one': serve open rows from SRAM while bitlines rest
idea: Stage crews change the set behind the closed curtain while actors play a scene 'in one' downstage. When a row stays open longer than about 200 ns, copy the sense-amp latch into a small per-bank SRAM row buffer, precharge the bitlines back to VDD/2, and serve further column hits from SRAM. The unselected cells on those bitlines then stop sitting at full-rail drain bias for microseconds, which removes bitline-dwell leakage under open-page traffic.
why: Fact 3: bitline dwell is an activity-dependent leakage driver that vendors guard-band. Removing it could relax refresh about 1.5x under heavy open-page loads, for about 0.5% of die area in SRAM.

title: Elimination-diet retention attribution: switch off one disturbance at a time
idea: An allergist finds the culprit by removing one food at a time. Drive commodity DDR5 from an open FPGA tester and remove one suspected leakage driver at a time (same-subarray bitline activity, neighbor-row activations, column traffic, I/O switching, thermal ripple) while refresh is held off for fixed windows. Then fit each row's failure rate to these factors to apportion tail leakage among hidden contributors. About $0.7M over 18 months yields per-vendor attribution tables that point design fixes at the biggest contributor.
why: Facts 3 and 9: refresh guard bands cover unknown, activity-dependent leakage. If 30-50% of tail failures prove activity-driven, targeted fixes or policies could relax refresh 1.5-2x.

title: Value-at-Risk retention sign-off simulates array transients, not DC corners
idea: Banks size capital with Monte Carlo Value-at-Risk over correlated shocks rather than one stacked worst case. Build an open sign-off tool that Monte-Carlos each cell's charge loss over a 64 ms window of realistic array events (bitline swings, off-rail bounce, passing-wordline pulses, thermal ripple) drawn from workload traces and convolved with leakage-tail statistics, and reports a 1e-9 'retention VaR'. Guard band is then spent only where transients actually stack. Budget is about $0.8M over 2 years with a university EDA group.
why: Facts 3 and 4: stacking DC worst cases over-guards refresh. Transient-aware sign-off could recover 20-40% of refresh interval, or justify a smaller cell.

title: WLTP-style drive cycle for DRAM retention specs under realistic traffic
idea: Car fuel-economy ratings became honest when the unrealistic NEDC lab cycle gave way to WLTP. Define a 'retention drive cycle' to propose to JEDEC and OCP: standard traffic, bitline-activity and thermal-ripple profiles applied during pause tests, so datasheets state retention under load rather than in an idle oven. For $1M over 24 months, build an open test rig, measure 30 part numbers, and submit the cycle.
why: Facts 3 and 4: idle-only specs hide activity-driven leakage and force blind over-refresh. An honest cycle lets load-robust parts ship with about 1.5x relaxed refresh and rewards vendors who fix hidden contributors.

title: Selenium toning for silicon: Se-bridged passivation of STI sidewalls
idea: Photographers selenium-tone silver prints so the image resists oxidation for centuries. After the STI etch, expose the trench sidewalls to H2Se or SeO2 vapor to form a sub-monolayer of Se bridging the dangling bonds (Se-passivated Si(100) shows very low interface-state density), then seal it under a low-temperature ALD SiO2 liner so the bridges survive. A university program of about $0.8M over 20 months measures gated-diode generation and STI-edge leakage against standard liners.
why: Fact 3: STI-sidewall interface states drive surface generation at storage junctions. If Se bridging cuts their density 3x, surface tail leakage falls 2-3x and refresh relaxes about 1.5-2x.

title: Post-exposure prophylaxis: early refresh for subarrays after long bitline dwell
idea: Clinicians give prophylaxis right after a known exposure instead of dosing everyone. A DDR5 controller tracks, per subarray (mapping reverse-engineered), the cumulative time any row has been held open with its bitlines at full rail. When that dwell budget is exceeded, it restores the subarray's other rows early with ACT/PRE, because their access transistors sat at full-rail drain bias. Only exposed subarrays get the extra dose, so the baseline refresh can follow the unexposed population; about $0.6M over 18 months on commodity parts.
why: Facts 3 and 9: bitline-dwell leakage is one reason refresh is guard-banded for everyone. Targeted early refresh could allow a 1.5-2x longer baseline tREFW for under 3% extra activations.

title: Bisque-fire the trench fill: purge flowable-oxide residues before liner seal
idea: Potters bisque-fire ware to drive out water and organics before glazing, or the glaze pinholes. Flowable-CVD STI fill keeps Si-H, N-H and carbon residues that end up against array sidewalls as border traps and fixed charge. Add a staged UV-ozone and steam 'bisque' cure below 450 C before the high-temperature densify, over a first ALD SiO2 skin liner, and run split lots at a 200 mm U.S. foundry to compare STI-edge leakage and VRT density (about $0.9M, 24 months).
why: Fact 3: STI-edge traps feed tail and VRT cells. A residue-free fill could halve STI-edge generation through a cheap process tweak.

title: Change-ringing refresh order spreads load across sub-wordline-driver stripes
idea: Change ringers follow methods such as plain hunt so that no bell sounds twice in the same place in a row. Reorder refresh so consecutive refresh activations never land in the same mat or sub-wordline-driver stripe within a short window, giving each stripe's off-rail and well time to recover before the next hit. This is a permuted refresh counter, prototyped as ACT/PRE-driven refresh from an FPGA controller and checked against retention under refresh-heavy load (about $0.4M, 12 months).
why: Fact 3: refresh bursts concentrated in one stripe raise off-rail bounce and transient leakage. Spreading them could trim activity-driven tail failures 20-50% and permit denser refresh bursts.

title: Fisher's Latin squares pick neighbor-pattern tests in a few passes
idea: R.A. Fisher's agricultural Latin-square trials compare every treatment against every neighbor using few plots. Generate retention-test data backgrounds as orthogonal or covering arrays over each cell's 8 physical neighbors, aware of true and anti cells, so every neighbor-state combination that drives cell-to-cell leakage appears in 6-8 passes instead of dozens. It is software-only on existing testers, about $0.3M over 12 months.
why: Facts 3 and 4: pattern-dependent retention forces long test suites and blind guard bands. Covering arrays could cut retention-test time about 3x, saving tester capital, while catching worst cases that march patterns miss.

title: Probe thermometer, not oven dial: test each die at its true temperature
idea: Cooks measure the meat, not the oven setting. During wafer-level pause tests, read each die's on-die thermal sensor, calibrated by a two-point check at sort, and correct every die's retention measurement to its actual junction temperature instead of trusting the chuck setpoint, whose die-to-die spread is about +/-2-3 C. Retention halves every 10 C or so, so that uncertainty alone costs about 20% guard band. This is a test-program change, about $0.4M over 12 months.
why: Facts 3 and 4: removing temperature uncertainty recovers about 20-30% of the refresh-spec guard band, available as longer tREFW or higher yield at the same spec.

title: Aviation-style confidential reporting of process-induced leakage incidents
idea: NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System gives pilots immunity for confidential near-miss reports, turning private mistakes into industry learning. Set up a legally protected third-party exchange where fabs, tool vendors and universities file anonymized reports of retention-tail excursions and their causes (charging events, contamination, recipe drift), with quarterly digests of root causes and fixes. About $0.8M over 2 years covers the secretariat, database and legal framework.
why: Facts 3 and 4: each fab rediscovers the same hidden leakage contributors. Shared incident learning could shorten tail-excursion fixes from months to weeks and speed new U.S. memory lines up the yield curve.

title: Sweating DIMMs: hydrogel coat evaporates moisture to clip thermal bursts
idea: Mammals sweat to dump heat during bursts of effort. Coat DIMM and HBM-adjacent heat spreaders with a LiCl-loaded polyacrylamide hydrogel that absorbs room humidity while idle and evaporates it during load spikes, absorbing about 2.3 kJ per gram of water and holding DRAM 5-10 C cooler through minutes-long bursts before recharging at idle. Prototype and rack trial cost about $0.5M over 18 months.
why: Fact 3: refresh doubles above 85 C and retention halves every 10 C or so. Clipping bursts 5-10 C avoids 2x refresh mode and adds about 1.5x margin, passively.

title: Hundred-year-flood statistics watch the leakage tail, not the mean
idea: Hydrologists set levee heights from extreme-value fits of annual floods, not from averages. Fit generalized-Pareto models to the worst 0.1% of per-wafer retention or leakage readings, and run statistical process control on the tail-shape and return-level parameters. A process drift that fattens the 1e-6 tail is then flagged lots before any mean metric moves. This is analytics on existing data, about $0.3M over 12 months.
why: Facts 3 and 4: tail excursions are caught late today, costing yield and forcing extra refresh guard band. Extreme-value monitoring could catch them 5-10x earlier.

title: Galvanic-isolation cleans stop metal ions plating onto storage junctions
idea: Shipbuilders and dentists keep dissimilar metals apart in an electrolyte so the less noble one does not dissolve. In DRAM wet cleans, exposed TiN, W, Mo and Ru wordline and contact metals form galvanic couples in dilute HF or SC1 that dissolve and redeposit metal ions onto nearby silicon, seeding junction leakage. Add azole or amine corrosion inhibitors and reorder steps so only one metal is ever exposed to a given clean, verified by TXRF and gated-diode leakage splits (about $0.6M, 18 months).
why: Fact 3: metal contamination at storage junctions creates deep-level tail cells. Removing a galvanic source could cut tail density 1.5-3x.

title: Non-stick cookware for implanters: beamline liners end energetic metal co-implants
idea: Cooks moved from reactive copper pans to inert liners so the food carries no metal. Ion implanters sputter Mo, W, Fe and Cr from arc chambers and apertures, and some of it is co-implanted at energy straight into the storage-junction depletion region, where gettering cannot pull it back out. Line the source, extraction and aperture parts with high-purity silicon or graphite and add an energy filter for the storage-node step, verified by TXRF/SIMS and junction-leakage splits (about $0.7M, 18 months).
why: Fact 3: energetic metals sit right where generation happens. Removing them could halve deep-level tail cells.

title: Overtraining warning: redesign burn-in that manufactures access-transistor traps
idea: Coaches know overtraining injures the athletes it was meant to toughen. Burn-in at high VPP and temperature screens infant mortality, but it also applies hot-carrier and bias-temperature stress to access-transistor gate edges, creating interface traps and VRT defects that later set the refresh rate. Split lots compare standard burn-in with a short, cooler, low-VPP, pattern-targeted recipe plus retention re-test, to find a recipe that screens defects without creating tail cells (about $0.5M, 18 months).
why: Facts 3 and 4: if burn-in adds even 20-30% of tail cells, a gentler recipe recovers that refresh margin and cuts burn-in oven hours, which are capital.

title: Military leapfrog: refresh one subarray while its neighbor serves reads
idea: Infantry leapfrog: one squad moves while the other covers. On commodity DDR4 and DDR5, an FPGA controller issues ACT-PRE-ACT sequences with deliberately shortened timing, so a refresh-target row in one subarray opens while the requested row in another subarray of the same bank is activated, hiding the refresh behind the access. The project characterizes which vendors and subarray pairs support this and builds a controller that hides most refresh (about $0.6M, 18 months).
why: Fact 3: refresh costs 10-20% of bandwidth at 32-64 Gb. Hiding 50-80% of it in parallel subarrays recovers most of that bandwidth with no new silicon.

title: Epidemiology case-control study pins tail excursions on process steps
idea: Epidemiologists find causes by matching cases to controls and comparing their exposures. Pair each tail-rich wafer with matched tail-normal wafers from the same lot, compare their chamber, queue-time and recipe histories with conditional logistic regression, and rank which step 'exposure' best explains the extra tail cells. It uses existing manufacturing-execution data: about $0.4M over 12 months to build and validate at one fab.
why: Facts 3 and 4: hidden process contributors are found by trial and error today. Matched-pair analysis could cut root-cause time 3-5x and shrink the leakage tail faster.

title: Sham-surgery split lots separate process handling from process chemistry
idea: Surgical trials use sham operations to separate the procedure's effect from the incision and anesthesia. For each suspect front-end step, run a sham split that goes through the same chamber load, pump-down, chucking and plasma-on time with the reactive chemistry switched off, so differences in the leakage tail are attributed to charging and handling versus chemistry. The campaign uses gated-diode and 1T1C test structures on a 200 mm U.S. line (about $0.6M, 18 months).
why: Fact 3: much of the tail may come from handling (charging, chuck contact, plasma UV) rather than chemistry. Sham controls aim fixes at the real cause, targeting about 2x tail reduction per corrected step.

title: ALARA radiation dose rules for e-beam inspection of DRAM arrays
idea: Radiologists keep X-ray dose 'as low as reasonably achievable'. Inline CD-SEM and e-beam inspection deposit electron dose into access-transistor gate oxides and STI liners at the wordline and storage-contact steps, creating trap precursors. Measure trap generation against landing energy and dose on test structures, then cap dose on product dies with low kV and sparse sampling, and move high-dose inspection to sacrificial monitor dies (about $0.5M, 18 months).
why: Fact 3: if metrology seeds even 10-20% of tail traps, capping dose recovers that refresh margin at no cost and also shortens metrology time.

title: Space-electronics edgeless gate: annular write transistor for gain-cell eDRAM
idea: Radiation-hard satellite chips use enclosed-layout (annular) transistors so that no channel edge touches the trench oxide. Draw the write transistor of logic-process 2T/3T gain cells as an annular device with the storage node at its center, removing the STI-edge parasitic channel and the narrow-width Vt roll-off that dominate its off-current. Tape out on SkyWater 130 nm and GF 22 nm MPWs and compare retention with standard layouts (about $0.6M, 18 months).
why: Fact 3 and U.S. manufacturability: STI-edge leakage can be about 10x the main-channel leakage in narrow devices. Edgeless write transistors could lengthen gain-cell retention 3-10x on U.S. logic fabs.

title: Irrigation anti-siphon valve: clamp bitline undershoot before it injects electrons
idea: Irrigation lines use anti-siphon valves so negative pressure cannot pull dirty water backward. When sense amps or equalizers ring, bitlines briefly undershoot below the p-well potential, forward-biasing bitline-contact junctions, which inject electrons that diffuse to neighboring storage nodes. Add a small active clamp per bitline pair and a soft-start on the sense-amp ground line, and quantify the retention gain on a 1T1C test array on a U.S. MPW (about $0.7M, 18 months).
why: Fact 3: injected minority carriers are an activity-dependent leakage source. Clamping undershoot could remove an estimated 10-30% tail component and harden the array against hammer-like injection.
